sections.section_title: The River and the Tree of Life
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit with leaves for the healing of the nations; the section describes the new creation's life-giving features rather than addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: No More Curse -- The Servants' Eternal Reign
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the abolition of the curse, the throne of God and the Lamb in the city, the servants' sacred worship-service, their seeing God's face, his name on their foreheads, the elimination of night, and their eternal reign.
sections.relevance: The passage describes the final, settled state of the redeemed in language of unrestricted permanence: the servants 'will see his face' (reversing the prohibition of Exodus 33:20), God's name is 'on their foreheads' (the permanent mark of belonging), and 'they will reign forever and ever' (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn, the strongest temporal expression in the document). The neutral reading notes that the reign progresses from temporal (a thousand years in 20:4, 6) to eternal (forever and ever in 22:5). This describes the ultimate state of the faithful as permanently secure. However, the passage describes the END state of those who have already overcome, not whether that state can be lost along the way. It addresses what the redeemed receive, not the conditions for arriving there.
key_phrases: his name will be on their foreheads
they will reign forever and ever
There will no longer be any curse

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the authentication of the document's words as faithful and true, with Christ declaring 'I am coming quickly' and pronouncing the sixth beatitude: blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book.
sections.relevance: The beatitude's condition is tērōn (present participle of tēreō, 'keeping, heeding, guarding') -- the same verb used in 1:3 and throughout the letters for active obedience. The neutral reading notes that this beatitude 'directly echoes the first' (1:3) and that 'keeping' means 'active, sustained obedience to what has been communicated.' Blessedness is conditional on ongoing heeding of the prophecy. This implies that the promised blessing is not automatically received but depends on continued response to the revelation.
key_phrases: Blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents John's second attempt to worship the angel and the second rebuke directing worship to God alone; the section addresses proper worship rather than the believer's standing.

The neutral reading presents the instruction not to seal the prophecy because the time is near, followed by the declaration that the wrongdoer will continue in wrong, the filthy in filth, the righteous in righteousness, and the holy in holiness; the section addresses the finality of present decisions and the urgency of the moment rather than directly addressing the permanence or conditionality of the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: Coming Soon with Reward -- The Alpha and Omega
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Christ's second declaration of imminent coming, with his reward to render to every person according to what they have done, followed by the comprehensive self-identification as Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end.
sections.relevance: The statement 'my reward is with me, to render to every man according to what he has done' (drawing on Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11) establishes a judgment-by-deeds framework. The neutral reading notes that the criterion is 'his work' (to ergon autou) -- 'what each person has done' -- and that 'the reward is not uniform,' with the overcomer inheriting the new creation (21:7) and the faithless receiving the second death (21:8). This is consistent with the deeds-based judgment of 20:12-13 and the 'I know your works' refrain throughout the letters. The passage implies that final outcome is determined by conduct, favoring conditionality.
key_phrases: my reward is with me, to render to every man according to what he has done
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end

sections.section_title: The Seventh Beatitude and the Final Exclusion
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the seventh and final beatitude declaring blessed those who wash their robes so that they may have the right to the tree of life and enter the city, contrasted with the excluded categories outside: dogs, sorcerers, immoral, murderers, idolaters, and all who love and practice lying.
sections.relevance: The present participle 'those who wash their robes' (hoi plynontes, ongoing action) makes access to the tree of life and entry into the city conditional on continuous robe-washing. The neutral reading connects this to 7:14, where the great multitude 'washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb,' and notes that the present participle 'indicates ongoing action -- not a single past event but a continuous practice.' The right (exousia) to the tree of life is not automatic but belongs to those who maintain the washed condition. The excluded categories (22:15) mirror 21:8 and represent participation in the beast's system. The passage directly addresses the conditions for access to eternal life and makes them ongoing rather than once-for-all, constituting one of the document's strongest conditional statements.
key_phrases: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life
and may enter by the gates into the city
Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the immoral persons

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus identifying himself as the root and descendant of David and the bright morning star, confirming his role as the one who sent his angel to testify to the assemblies; the section is a Christological self-identification rather than a statement about the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Spirit and the Bride Say 'Come'
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the Spirit and the bride issuing the invitation 'Come,' extending the invitation to every hearer and to the thirsty to take the water of life without cost; the section is an open evangelistic invitation expressing the free availability of salvation rather than directly addressing whether the believer's standing is permanent or conditional.

The neutral reading presents the solemn warning that if anyone adds to the prophecy, God will add the plagues to him, and if anyone takes away from it, God will take away his part from the tree of life and from the holy city.
sections.relevance: The passage directly states that God will 'take away his part (meros) from the tree of life and from the holy city.' The neutral reading notes that meros ('part, share, portion') is the same word used in 21:8 for the cowardly and faithless having their 'part' in the lake of fire, and in 20:6 for having 'a part' in the first resurrection. The verb aphelei ('will take away') implies removal of something previously possessed or available. The person whose share is removed forfeits 'membership in the community' the prophecy addresses. This is a listed proof-text (Rev 22:19) cited for conditionality, and the neutral reading supports the conventional use: the text explicitly states that a person's share in the tree of life and the holy city can be taken away by God as a consequence of specific conduct. This directly addresses whether standing before God is permanent or conditional and answers that it is conditional.
key_phrases: if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the tree of life and from the holy city
if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues which are written in this book

sections.section_title: 'Come, Lord Jesus' -- The Final Exchange and Benediction
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus's final declaration 'Yes, I am coming quickly,' John's response 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus,' and the closing benediction of grace; the section is the document's concluding exchange and benediction rather than a statement about the believer's standing.
